To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the vascular wall responds to mechanical forces with a variety of adaptive mechanisms, which include the synthesis of new proteins.

1) the endothelial cell is a mechanosensor and that it can sense both the shear stress and the stretch; 2) the endothelial cells are able to adapt to these stimuli by modifying their phenotype and their functions, in particular by increasing the expression of genes involved in the control of the blood coagulation; 3) the endothelial and the smooth muscle cells have in common the same mechanoreceptors, i.e. the stretch activated ion channels and focal adhesion structures

the endothelial cells and vascular smooth muscle cells respond to changes in mechanical stress by activating specific signal transduction pathways, leading to changes in gene expression, which are essential for vascular remodeling.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular mechanisms involved in the adaptation of the cardiovascular system to the mechanical forces acting on the vessel wall. M. L. Tremblay Departement
the study of mechanical signals and their transduction into biochemical signals in vascular cells, and the consequences of the biochemical response on the cell phenotype and the extracellular matrix.
the study of the mechanisms of adaptation of vascular smooth muscle cells to mechanical stress and the mechanisms of transmission of the mechanical signal to the nucleus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the mechanical signals transmitted by the endothelium to the smooth muscle cells are responsible for the regulation of the contractile tone of the vessel, and the endothelium is responsible for the remodeling of the vessel wall.
the endothelial cells are the main target of shear stress and stretch and the vascular smooth muscle cells are the main targets of stretch.
the endothelial cells are able to sense the fluid shear stress and the stretch, and to respond to these stimuli by a complex and well coordinated series of events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the endothelium senses the shear stress and converts it to a biochemical signal that is then transduced into the nucleus to regulate the expression of specific genes.
the mechanical signals are transduced by the endothelial cells through focal adhesion and cytoskeletal proteins, leading to the expression of genes involved in vascular remodeling.
the mechanical signals are transmitted through focal adhesion sites to the nucleus, where they induce gene expression and the production of proteins that regulate vascular remodeling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cell is the key to understanding how the body works and how it responds to disease, injury and drugs.
the mechanical environment of the cells is a critical regulator of the cell phenotype.
the mechanical properties of the cell membrane are a critical determinant in the ability of a cell to sense mechanical forces and transmit them to the cytoskeleton.
